utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Today we have the return of Paul Davies. As the Court recalls, Paul Davies was the ITN reporter who came early in the case and, because of a change in schedule, had to leave during the middle of cross-examination. The Defence will continue cross-examining. However, during the examination the issue was raised as to the providence of the videotape that was in the possession of the Prosecutor. That's at page 638 and again at 655. We have received a report from Ellen Gardner, who is from the director of operations from the Linden Production Company out of Los Angeles, the former director of operations of that company who provided that tape, and we have a copy of that report which provides the providence of that film. In addition, we've been notified that, through the Victims and Witnesses a few weeks ago, that the witness has a copy, a full copy, with those additional seconds from the beginning and the end of the tape. Where we can't speak with him directly, we don't know if he has it with him today. Could we request the Court to inquire if he does have that and could he turn it over to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the witness be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Davies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: May I first remind you of the affirmation you made before the Tribunal to tell the truth, which is still applicable, and thank you for being able to return. I gather that you may have secured a copy of the original recording without deletions. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is. It's in the witness room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I wonder perhaps if you are still being cross-examined at the first break, which is probable, if you would be able to bring that with you when you come back after the break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that very easily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, I think it's a matter of continuing the cross-examination. Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Davies. We will continue from where we stopped. Tell me: Do you know Phil Davison, a British freelance journalist?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that he was in Dubrovnik for a while in 1991 during the period that you were in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. Yes, I met him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Phil Davison was in Dubrovnik from mid-October until around the 14th of November, 1991. Did you find him there because he was staying at the Argentina Hotel?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I met him at the Argentina Hotel and talked to him on a number of occasions. I do know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you have a high regard for him as a colleague, a journalist, and do you think highly of his professional work?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's a respected newspaper journalist, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Since he came to Dubrovnik before you, did Phil Davison familiarise you with the situation in Dubrovnik when you arrived there? Did he have things to tell you?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would have spoken, I'm sure, because I know him. We would certainly have spoken. He was there a little time before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I assume that he provided you with the first information you received concerning Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. The first information I received about Dubrovnik would have been on the -- when we arrived at the port and there were some other journalists there at the time who I knew -- who I'd met on previous assignments who I spoke to. I think they were the people who gave me the first information about their experience in Dubrovnik. But certainly at some stage later I would have spoken to Mr. Davison, certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Sir, last time you told us that you came to Dubrovnik with a crew that consisted of the producer of the -- sound editor, film editor, and Nigel Thomson, cameraman. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: However, Mr. Phil Davison says that in mid-October he came to Dubrovnik with John Jones and Nigel Thomson in order to work for Independent.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that -- there's obviously a mix-up of information there because Nigel Thomson is the cameraman who is employed by my company. In fact, he was my partner for a number of years and we travelled together, so there's obviously some confusion about the date when people arrived there. Certainly Phil Davison and Nigel Thomson would have been there together for a long period of the assignment, but they didn't arrive together.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In your statement when you mentioned a colleague of yours, a journalist who was wounded by sniper fire near the Argentina Hotel, I presume that you meant the journalist Phil Davison. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, yes. He received a wound -- I think it was to his ankle in the -- I can't remember the exact date, but it was in that period of time around the 9th, 10th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was Phil Davison treated at the Dubrovnik hospital?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, but I wasn't -- I wasn't there. I didn't see it. I know he received some treatment and he was med-evac'd, taken out of Dubrovnik at the first opportunity, which I think was on the 13th of November when the ferry was allowed to leave the port. This is just my memory. I certainly didn't witness him receiving any treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You testified in the Milosevic trial, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: While giving evidence in the Milosevic trial, you mentioned a colleague of yours who had been in hospital for a longer period of time. Is that Phil Davison?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us then who this was.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not certain. The only -- two of my colleagues needed -- that's of the journalists, needed medical treatment. One would have been Phil Davison. Another colleague, a gentleman called Sandy McIntyre, was also at the hospital for a brief time. I may have mentioned him. Certainly none of my colleagues were badly hurt and nobody needed to stay in hospital for any length of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. So both Phil Davison and your other colleague, Sandy McIntyre, were in hospital in Dubrovnik in that period from October to December 1991. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult for me to answer exact yes or no answers to that. Certainly I believe Phil Davison received treatment at the hospital. And the other gentleman, Sandy McIntyre, was at the hospital. There was an incident, I think it was some shelling, around the hospital, and he hurt his leg. He wasn't wounded by the actual shelling; he hurt his leg, I think falling, and received some treatment there. I don't think either of them were actually kept in hospital for any length of time. By any length of time, I don't think either of them actually sort Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of went into a bed, I think they were just treated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Also in the Milosevic trial during your testimony, you said that this colleague of yours who was in hospital saw a mobile mortar position and fire being opened from that position, which is in the immediate vicinity of the hospital. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't recollect saying that. No, I don't remember saying that somebody in the hospital witnessed mortars being fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did Phil Davison ever tell you that on the ramparts and within the Old City walls, the Croats had mortars and that the JNA targeted them with missiles, wired missiles?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't tell me that. And he wouldn't -- he wouldn't have been in a position to do that because at the time that he was -- at the time that the wire missiles were fired, he had been injured and he was restricted to the hotel. He didn't -- he stopped roaming the city after he was wounded, and certainly -- the day the wire missiles were fired was the 12th of November, and he was not mobile at that time. So I don't believe he would have been on the walls of the Old City or been in a position to see that there were mortars on the walls of the Old City.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did Phil Davison tell you or did you see or hear for yourself that Croat soldiers had a machine-gun nest in the attic of the Argentina Hotel and that they were firing from there, and that Phil Davison complained to the hotel management on account of that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Phil Davison didn't tell me that at that time, no. I have spoken to him in the 12 years or so since then, and he has told me that he did complain about gun positions being placed very briefly around the hotel. I believe this was possibly at the time when he was restricted to the hotel and was spending his day there. I think he -- if I recollect that conversation, he also said that the monitors, the European Union monitors, were also concerned that this should not happen. And my understanding was that the situation changed. I don't know whether the gun position that he was talking about was one that was being used, or whether he'd just seen some military activity there. It seemed to be a brief position that -- a brief situation that disappeared after complaints were made. This isn't anything that I witnessed or my team witnessed at all, it was something that I believe Phil Davison saw when he was restricted to the Hotel Argentina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davies, then that is a mortar position near the Argentina Hotel. And Phil Davison said that it was visible to all, that is to say that it was not concealed. That's the position you referred to a short while ago. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I think what I was referring to was whether or not a -- I forget the words you used, a machine-gun nest was being placed, or something like that. I wasn't aware you were talking about a mortar position. On the subject of mortar positions near the Argentina Hotel, this is something that you and I discussed last time and I told you that, yes, I was aware, as indeed most of the journalists who were staying in the hotel were aware, that at certain times mortars were fired from positions near the Argentina Hotel. This appeared to be a mobile mortar unit that was firing from a position as close as it could get to the surrounding military and then moving very quickly to another location or to a safer location, having exposed itself. This seemed to be pretty much the main military tactic of the people who were defending the city of Dubrovnik, using a very limited number of mortars and, I believe, a limited number of small artillery pieces to fire and then to move to new positions and to try not to be hit by returning fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Davies. Tell me, please, during your stay in Dubrovnik, did you witness any situations of unnecessary provocations coming from town, provocations that were intended to cause the JNA to fire? Can you remember any such thing?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't. Again, that's not to say that it didn't happen, but I didn't witness anything that I thought was provocative action. But quite often the first indication that you would get that the peace was being broken again was the sound of distant gunfire or shelling. And then it either came closer to you or you went to look where was being hit. You wouldn't necessarily be in a position to judge what had provoked what or who had fired the first shot. The best you could do is judge what you saw, and in every case what you saw was a very one-sided conflict with one side having far more weapons and inflicting far more damage than the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In the Milosevic case, you said that the JNA targeted the Croatian artillery, which was hidden in the town park from where they were shooting at the JNA. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me where the park is.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the park I'm referring to is in the area north of the Old City. It's a -- the area I'm referring to is a wooded area that is alongside the coast and between the Old City and - I'm just trying to think about the landmarks - the hospital, say. But not directly alongside either of those two that I've mentioned or indeed in the grounds of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: While you were in Dubrovnik, did you hear about a park called Gradac and Boskovicev Park or some other park?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the names of the parks, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask the usher to show the witness Exhibit D28, please, Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davies, this is a picture from Boskovicev Park from the film that has been introduced into evidence. This is a still from that footage. Were you ever a witness of any similar situation while you were in Dubrovnik? Did you ever see anything like this? Or perhaps you know this man?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I certainly don't know the man, but I witnessed something similar with a small team that had a mortar that looked similar to this that were moving around. And I know of journalists who witnessed mortars being fired from wooded areas. So, yes, I've seen something similar to this, not -- I don't know where this particular park is. I wouldn't be able to say I saw anything like this happening in this park, but I saw generally similar things happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the examination-in-chief you said that the Croats had cannons of smaller calibres, smaller calibre weapons and they were on wheels, that you saw these mobile cannons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I have no objection, but as a point of assistance, if we can call it, when counsel refers to the Milosevic trial or our own trial here and the prior testimony, could they please refer to a certain page so we could follow along. We have the transcripts here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we're not talking about the Milosevic trial at the moment. I'm referring to this witness's examination-in-chief. As to the testimony in the Milosevic case, my previous two questions were based on that, Your Honours. But perhaps after the break I will return to that because I didn't comment the witness's negative answer or response to my question that referred to the Milosevic case, because I do indeed have the transcript from that trial before me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Mr. Rodic. It would be useful to everybody, when you're referring to particular passages, to give a page reference. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: That means, Mr. Davies, as I was saying a moment ago -- I asked you a question, but I'll repeat. And it was this: During the examination-in-chief in this case, you testified that the Croats had cannons of a smaller calibre and that they were on wheels, mounted on wheels, and this made them mobile. Now, I should like to ask you to take Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. a look at a photograph and tell me whether those are the types of cannon that you mentioned. And it is Exhibit P32.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, once again, could he please refer us to which page he is discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was testimony during the examination-in-chief, Mr. Weiner. I can't give you a page number for every question of mine. The examination-in-chief was conducted by Ms. Somers. She is absent, and I understand why.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I understand that this is more of a generalised question, so I won't object to that. But if he's planning to impeach a witness with any prior statement or question him about some certain statement, I think he should refer to a certain page so we know that the language is ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That would be desirable, Mr. Rodic, as you go along. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think we've put things upside down. It is not my intention to discredit the witness through my question, to impeach him, but I mentioned something that the witness himself said during the examination-in-chief, and all I'm asking him to do now is to compare that part of his testimony with the piece of evidence that we're going to put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The point being made is a simple one, Mr. Rodic: It would be of considerable convenience to the Chamber and to the Prosecution if when you say, You said this in your examination-in-chief, if you could say, That appeared at, and give the reference to the transcript. Now, if you haven't prepared to do that at the moment, if you could try to do that as you progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise to the usher, but may we have D32, Exhibit D32, and it is the cannon in Gradac Park, and that's what it says on the still.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you see the wheels on this photograph through the bushes, the wheels of this cannon?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see them, but I can -- I can imagine where they are and with the sort of piece that it appears to be. But I can't actually see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you see a cannon on this picture?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Does that roughly correspond to a small-calibre cannon of the type that you yourself saw? Would you say that the one you saw was similar to this one here?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't think I could in honesty judge it just from being able to see this. I mean, it might have been something similar to this but it's difficult to judge the scale of this particular weapon without seeing something to judge it with.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to thank the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davies, when you spoke about the warehouse of the JNA, the ammunitions warehouse at Zarkovica - and we can see that from the footage we saw - you noted that there had been a major explosion. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly there was an explosion that we could witness from the Old City.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was there any ricochetting, or rather, were any projectiles flying to and from town, parts of the exploded projectiles from the area and mines?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so. It is possible that some may have exploded towards Dubrovnik, but it was quite some distance away, a distance that only on this one occasion, which was the significance of the explosion, had the Croatian forces manage to hit the top of Zarkovica. And in order to do so, they appeared to have moved their weaponry as close as they possibly could, which was somewhere in the region of the Belvedere Hotel. And even then, most of what they'd been firing at the JNA position was falling short. Then there was this one explosion that was obviously a hit, and it was more than just an impact. It was bigger than that and seemed to be one or two smaller explosions afterwards, which is why we judged it to have hit munitions or something of this type. I don't believe that what was fired, what exploded on Zarkovica could have reached the centre of Dubrovnik and certainly not caused lots of damage. But it is possible that something might have exploded in the Dubrovnik direction. Certainly, as witnesses, we weren't thinking that we were in danger from anything that was exploding up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: As I've said, in your report we can see the actual point when the ammunition at Zarkovica was hit, that particular moment. Now, before that hit, did you know that that was the target of the Croatian forces, of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably had an idea that it might be the target because, first of all, fire was coming into Dubrovnik from that position. It was a position we were watching because there were big guns on top of it that were firing into Dubrovnik. And secondly, because we had already witnessed explosions on the hillside below the JNA position, as the Croatians were returning fire. So it was an area that was obviously of interest to us, and that's why we were filming it. We weren't aware that there was any specific military operation that was going to target the top of the position at Zarkovica. In fact, we weren't even -- we weren't with -- we weren't with anybody at that stage, we were just on the ramparts, filming what we could see from there. And most of the action, if you like, that was happening at that time seemed to be centred on the gun positions on the top of Zarkovica that were firing into Dubrovnik and then the attempts to return fire on them, one of which succeeded.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: That means that you were in the Old Town, since you managed to tape that hit?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were in the -- on the walls and on the walls that were closest to Zarkovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In your film, several seconds later -- several seconds after that hit at Zarkovica, we can see five people in the Old Town up by the wall, and of that two men are wearing uniforms and carrying weapons. Did you film that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's in the footage in that film, yes, we did film it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You also said that on the 13th of November, that is to say after those three or four days of fighting that you describe, that you toured the Old Town and that you had the opportunity of seeing a projectile embedded in the wall in the port which had not exploded. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should now like to ask the usher once again to show the witness Exhibit P69. It is Prosecution Exhibit Number 69.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: This is the Old Town, the part by the port. Can you recognise the projectile embedded in the wall towards the bottom of this photograph?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see a projectile. I wouldn't say that I could recognise it. I don't know if it's one that I've seen before or -- but there is what appears to be -- it is a very grainy picture, but there is something that appears to be sticking in the stone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Well, do you allow for the possibility, according to your recollections, that what you testified about, about embedded projectiles sticking into the wall and not having exploded in the port, that this could be that situation or a similar one?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: He's asking if he allows for the possibility that this could be the embedded projectile that he mentioned, and that's just asking the witness to speculate or to assume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think not, Mr. Weiner. Thank you. Carry on, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davies, can you answer my question, please.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that that is the one that I saw. My memory is that there was more than one in any case. Is it something similar? It may be something similar. We saw pieces of missiles that hadn't exploded, some of which were embedded in stone, and that appears to be something embedded in stone. So if that makes it similar, then possibly it's similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Davies. Also, when you toured the Old Town on that day, the 13th of November, you said that the damage to the Old Town was concentrated in the southern sections mostly, the southern part of the Old Town. Can you explain why that was?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can offer an opinion or I could speculate. The damage that we saw appeared to be concentrated on that day on the area of the Old Town that appeared to have taken the greater part of the bombardment. And that was the southern side of Dubrovnik, and in particular, around the small old port.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When we talk about the south side, could that also relate to the ramparts, the walls around the Old Town, the southern section facing the sea and that part of town from the south closest to the sea? I'm referring to the Old Town, of course, that section of the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The section of the walls that we're talking about are the -- is the side of the Old Town that is closest to Zarkovica, closest to the Hotel Argentina, that side, and that was the side of Dubrovnik from which we witnessed the missiles being fired over the water and against the walls. And we witnessed so many impacts against the walls, so I -- some fell short and hit boats and what have you outside the walls, some went over and caused explosions inside. But that would appear to be the reason why a lot of the damage was concentrated on that particular area at the south side.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davies, a witness from Dubrovnik who testified before this Honourable Trial Chamber said that he saw a position of the Croatian army, positions up above the Adriatic motorway, the main road, and the northern ramparts of the Old Town. Were you aware of that? That means between the northern walls of the Old Town and the motorway, that the Croatian army had its positions there. Since you moved around the ramparts in that general walled-in area, did you happen to notice any positions of that type?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't, and I spent a lot of time there, but I wasn't there all the time, obviously. But no, I didn't. If we had spotted military positions on the walls or within the Old City, it would have been a major part of the report that we put together. And we didn't see it and we were there many days and we didn't see it and it wasn't a part of the report. That's -- the reason it wasn't in the report is we didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Sir -- Mr. Davies, I don't think you understood me. Your answer to my question seems to imply that I asked you about the inner portions of the Old Town, about the area within the Old Town. That's not what I was actually asking you. The ramparts, the wall around the Old Town, from the north, on the north side, looking towards the hill. And there we have the main road. So my witness -- my question was that the witness before you saw between the walls and the main road, which doesn't mean the inner parts of the town, it means outside, between the outside walls on one side and the hill on the other and the road, that there were Croatian army positions in between.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand the question. I didn't see those positions, and again the answer would apply that had I seen those positions, we would have filmed them and they would have been in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned mortars on trucks that were moving in order to get close to the targets and JNA positions, could you tell me what part of town you saw that in?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it -- I can remember two occasions, though it's a long time ago now, but I can remember two occasions. One occasion was close to the new port, the Gruz area. And another occasion was in the region of -- I can't remember the hotel's name now, but it's the hotel that is between the Old City and the Hotel Argentina, there is a hotel. It was in disrepair at the time; nobody was in it. And I saw a truck with what appeared to be mobile mortars close to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is this perhaps the Excelsior Hotel?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: It -- I think it probably is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: With this truck and mortars, they were moving about. As soon as they would fire, they would move from those positions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned that the Croats had a mortar position near the Belvedere Hotel and that they were shooting towards Zarkovica and that more than one time they engaged a mortar near the Hotel Argentina and that they would move positions as they moved rapidly along the coast. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, yes, that was my understanding. We weren't able to follow them and to track down their movements precisely, but that seemed to be the tactic they were using and that was also the understanding that other journalists who saw things from time to time had.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I think that I already asked you this last time, but do you perhaps have such scenes recorded on camera?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: You did ask me, and the answer is no. I haven't any scenes recorded on camera of the mortars being moved or indeed fired. I do have -- I did film the effects of them being fired, but we were never able to be in a position to film the actual firing of the weapons. It was quite secretive and also very, very brief. You heard the noise, it had happened, and then they moved. My understanding from talking to some of the Croatian military was that it was for two reasons, one being that they exposed themselves to return fire, the other that they had so few mortars that that was the way that they could best use them, by firing them from one position and then moving very quickly on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Then, if I understood this correctly, in terms of assessing the situation itself, this has to do with a description of the truck that is mobile, it has a mortar mounted on it; once it fires, it moves away. So the same tactics like with the mortars that are on land, and then they are moved away soon after they're fired. Right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In the statement you gave to the investigators, on page 8 in the last paragraph of the statement, you say: "I remember that an anti-aircraft gun was mounted on a truck and moved from one place to another. I assume that they were moving it about from one place to another so that the enemy would not hit it. The Croats tried to make an armoured vehicle by themselves by welding some metal sheets on a truck, but obviously this was not very successful."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that they do not have the original text.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is D35. Could the usher please assist us with that. Could the witness please see this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is this the anti-aircraft gun mounted on a truck, the one that you talked about in your statement to the investigator?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to ask for P24, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davies, can you see on the lower photograph this armoured vehicle. Is that it? Is that the armoured vehicle, the one they called Majsan?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be. My memory was of the front not being quite as professional looking as that. I think possibly that it's not. The one that I saw was a cruder machine with the -- with the metal welded I think at the front. It was straight up as opposed to on a slant. That looks a little bit more sophisticated than the one that I saw. It also appears to be going, which the one that I saw was having huge difficulty in functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Davies. When you mentioned a short while ago the photograph I showed you, the anti-aircraft gun mounted on a truck, can you tell us where you actually had the opportunity of seeing that, at which positions? So which positions in terms of the town itself, where did you notice this truck with mounted anti-aircraft guns?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you with 100 per cent accuracy. I believe that it was somewhere in the new part of Dubrovnik. It might have been by a police station, because it was certainly by a police station I saw the armoured vehicle that I referred to. When I saw the vehicle that appeared to have an anti-aircraft gun on top of it, it wasn't being fired. And I think that's about as much as I can tell you about it. I also think I saw it once or twice in different places, but I didn't see it being fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon, Your Honour. The accused is complaining that he cannot hear the interpretation coming from the booth, so could I please ask the interpreters of the booth to say something so that he could check this. Thank you. It seems to be working now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Also, this anti-aircraft gun mounted on a truck, I assume that it was fired like the weapons that you described to us a short while ago, that is to say that they would open fire and then move away quickly. I assume that this also pertained to the anti-aircraft gun, right, this one?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're assuming and I would assume as well, but it is only an assumption. All I can add is that I can recall at a time when Dubrovnik was being bombed from the air that we heard what sounded like anti-aircraft fire being directed towards the planes that were bombing. But we didn't actually see the weapon that was firing at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I'm not mistaken, you've repeated several times already that it was impossible to catch the Croats in action because they were moving from one place to another very quickly. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be one reason why we couldn't film them in action. Another would be that it was much easier to film the attack that was coming from the other side because there was so much more of it. There was a lot of the attack that was coming from the other side that we also couldn't film because people were doing things very quickly. But because there was so much more of it, we were able to record it. So those would be the two reasons, I would say, we weren't able to film the Croats in action other than to see, on occasions, the impacts from mortars and artillery that they were firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You also said several times that you did not manage to film the moment when the Croat artillery would fire, but you did have the opportunity of filming their action in terms of the effects of that firing. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right. And to explain that, the first time usually that you would realise that there was fire coming out of the city was when you saw the impact, and that was the time that you pointed the camera in that direction, and if it happened again, then you filmed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, you mentioned that at your hotel there were some people from UNESCO, too. Do you know any of their names, perhaps, or do you remember what they looked like?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly don't remember their names, and as far as what they looked like, if they appeared on the reports that we made, then it would be easy to recognise them. But other than that, no, I don't memorise the faces of these people. We were just aware that some of them had been staying there and that there were various flags flying over the hotel, which also indicated the nationalities and roles of some of the people that were staying there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davies, do you remember how many representatives there were from UNESCO at the time when you were there?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: One of the representatives of UNESCO, Dr. Colin Kaiser, who testified before this Honourable Trial Chamber, mentioned that on his way to Dubrovnik, that is to say before he arrived, already in Zagreb he saw some ITN footage. And on it he saw the UNESCO flag on the fort on Srdj. Did you actually film that? Are you aware of this situation?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I'm not aware of -- of that particular flag. There was very large UNESCO flags over the Old City. I'm not sure that I recall a flag on top of Srdj.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was there a flag perhaps that was up there and that was removed later while the ones in town stayed on?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You were in Dubrovnik from the 31st of October until the 21st of November, 1991, if I'm not mistaken. Right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And after that you did not go back to Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not for a long time. I've only been back to Dubrovnik once since 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davies, how come there were people from UNESCO at the hotel, then, in view of the fact that they first came to Dubrovnik only on the 28th and 29th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. As I said, my understanding was that the hotel was used as a base for the monitoring gentlemen and UNESCO and also some nationalities as a temporary consulate. That was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davies, you also said in your statement given to the investigators, on page 10 in the first paragraph, the last sentence, you say: "I know that UNESCO representatives were also in town, but I don't know anything about them." That is your statement made on the 18th and 19th of January, 2001. Do you remember having stated that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It sounds familiar. And it was my understanding that UNESCO representatives were in town and, as you can see, I said I don't know anything about them, which explains why, when you asked me if I remembered any names or remembered any faces, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And do you know what their role was and what the point of their stay was in Dubrovnik and in the Old Town, of these people from UNESCO, that is?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I mean, obviously if I don't remember meeting them, I wouldn't necessarily know what the business was. My understanding, again, was that there were UNESCO representatives, and I was aware of the UNESCO link with Dubrovnik from the flags that were flying. That was really the sum of my knowledge of the UNESCO side of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what kind of flags these were.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were large blue and white UNESCO flags.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Where were they placed?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be specific about that. They were placed very, very prominently on high positions over the Old City, but I can't tell you which building or which rampart or whatever they were flown from, but they were very, very visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Mr. Davies, it seems to me that you are now circumventing the issue, because if I say that Dr. Colin Kaiser came with his colleagues and then placed UNESCO flags, is it possible that you saw UNESCO flags before he had actually come and put them there?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't have seen the specific flags that he placed before he placed them there. All I can tell you is that I recall seeing the UNESCO flags, blue and white flags, and even made references to the fact that Dubrovnik was a protected site in the reports that I was making at the time, and that isn't knowledge I would have gone to Dubrovnik with.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on. During the examination-in-chief, you also described your own movements about the Old Town, and you said that the Old City walls were a place with a good view of the surrounding area. Did you say something to that effect?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether it was precisely for that reason that there were observation points on the old walls?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would imagine that it would be an obvious place to observe, certainly to observe to the south. But again, I do have to say that I didn't witness military activity on those walls.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, would this be a good moment to take the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rodic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic -- I'm sorry, I didn't see you there, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No problem. Just a matter of logistics. The witness brought two tapes with him. He has one in his possession and one has been given to the audio/video room. They have to convert it to our system, which they say can be done very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Hopefully that may occur in the course of the evidence. There is every sign that it will, judging from the nod of the head from the video booth. Thank you. Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davies, you also mentioned the fact that with you in the Hotel Argentina there were also some observers from the European Community. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right. They had their office in the hotel and they were staying in the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You also said that you socialised with them. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a degree. I mean, we didn't have close friendships, but they would be -- at the end of the day they might be in the bar as well and we would talk occasionally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember any of those observers? Could you tell us their names, perhaps, where they were from.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't. They -- it was a multinational team. I think I can remember an Italian and that's as far as it goes, I fear. I certainly don't recall any of their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: When the shelling took place and there was an exchange of fire, did the observers use the shelters?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall seeing the observers in the shelters at the times that we visited them. They had their own duties, tasks, to perform during the day, observing, monitoring what was happening, and at times I believe trying to assist with any cease-fire arrangements. So it wasn't that they were just in one place and therefore would quite clearly have to go to a particular shelter when the firing started. But in answer to your question, no, I don't recall seeing them in the underground shelters. I do recall seeing them taking a much cruder form of shelter at times when the shelling was in and around the Hotel Argentina when people were going down to the basement of the hotel, and I can visualise some pictures that we took of some of the observers sheltering under the tables and still continuing whatever work it was that they were doing at that time. But again, in reply to your first question, I don't recall seeing them in the official underground shelters, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Unless I'm mistaken, during the shelling you at certain moments were outside the hotel. That means you were moving round the town of Dubrovnik, or round the Old Town; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. We learned that there were three or four places that gave good views of different areas, and we would spend quite a lot of our time in those areas if we didn't have a specific other job to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: On those occasions, did you ever happen to see any of the observers from the European Community moving around those parts of town, of the town of Dubrovnik, the broader Dubrovnik area or in the narrower Old Town part that you were able to see?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember doing so. No, I don't remember seeing them. I'm not sure that we would do a lot of the time, because from some of these vantage positions they were deliberately chosen as being places where a camera would get a very good top view of things that were happening and you wouldn't necessarily see all the movement on the ground of what was happening. But no, I don't recall seeing them in and around the town while the shelling was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you remember where the best vantage point, as you said, was; the best in terms of seeing a lot from that position?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would depend on where the fighting was concentrated or where the shelling was concentrated, and the two main positions were either on the ramparts of the Old City or, particularly in the earlier stages of our stay there, on one of the roads that ran at the top of Dubrovnik and was almost into the side of Srdj so that you were looking down -- you could look down and see the Old Town, but you could also see the new areas which took most of the attack in the early days before the 11th and 12th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, were you ever in a position to see or to film any large explosions in the warehouse in the port of Gruz?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: We filmed the immediate aftermath of the explosions. I don't think we actually filmed the impacts. I think we were doing something else or filming the shelling in a different area, became aware that the port of Gruz had been hit, and went there. And on a number of occasions we arrived there while warehouses were burning, ships were burning, and damage of that sort, which we filmed and broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So that means you didn't have the opportunity of seeing this directly, an explosion itself, in the warehouses in the port of Gruz in November 1991.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see the moment that a shell exploded and started an explosion and fire. As I say, I did film the immediate aftermath but not the actual impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps happen to hear that in one of those warehouses there was ammunition stored, which the Croats procured for their own purposes?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear that, and I wouldn't know whether it's true or false. I saw a lot of wood burning. Some of the warehouses contained wood and I was able to actually see for myself what was burning there, but I didn't either see or hear that any munitions had been hit in the port.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, with the European observers, did you exchange information, were you able to receive information from them about what was going on or could you give them any information? Was there this exchange of information as to what each of you saw while moving around town?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: On an unofficial basis there was some exchange of information. There wasn't -- there was no official format for either reporting to them what we'd seen or indeed learning from them what they'd seen. Occasionally, if there was any involvement in cease-fire talk or -- we'd be told something about it, but most of what we learned from them was talk at the end of the day, possibly in the restaurant or the bar, but nothing official.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I'm not insisting, nor do I think that there were any official exchanges. I'm asking you about your unofficial conversations, because I assume that, as a journalist yourself, you use observers as a source of information.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they're willing to become that source of information, yes. And there was an exchange some days, usually in the hotel at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps know how they came by their information about what was going on in the Dubrovnik region?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about the Crisis Staff in Dubrovnik during the time you spent there?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not by that name. So perhaps if you wanted to explain what it was they did, then possibly I was aware of it, but I wasn't aware of anything called the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff in Dubrovnik dealt with the care of citizens, the citizens of the town, ensuring supplies, dealing with entrances and exits from Dubrovnik, related to defence matters; all this came within their work. And they also took part in negotiations with the JNA. Does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, certainly all of those things happened and people were involved in organising it. I didn't know they went by the name Crisis Staff, but yes, those activities happened and we were sufficiently aware of most of them to be involved in filming distribution of food and things like that around the town. So yes, there were people doing that sort of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And in the Argentina Hotel, for example, were there any representatives of Dubrovnik who would be informing the observers directly about some matter?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a -- an information office, I suppose you would call it, which was manned by local Croatian people who would give the journalists and the observers their views or information on what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you use them, too, as a source of information?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would listen to what they had to say, but it was a very biased source of information. And we were aware of that from the start. Sometimes it could be useful; for instance, in knowing when food, water, distribution was happening and that sort of thing, or even if you were to be reporting that one side in the conflict is claiming that it's running short of whatever essential supplies. But we were always aware -- it was very, very plain to see that it was a service set up to put across the Croatian side and it had to be treated accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you say "bias," this Croatian office in the Argentina Hotel which gave out information, when you use the word "biased" I don't assume that related to the information you received with respect to the distribution of food, water, bread, et cetera. I assume that when you talk about bias you refer to something else in some other area. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking primarily of other areas where you would suspect or at least need to treat the information you were being given knowing that it was coming from one particular side and one particular view. But in areas like food distribution, water, et cetera, obviously that was happening and you could see that, and that made it easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether I was clear enough. The distribution of water and food, the locations, the time and place this was done, this distribution, I personally don't see that there is any great scope for manipulation in that particular area. And since you mentioned biased, I would like to ask you what information that referred to, how did you come to conclude at certain points in time that there might have been a bias on the part of the side giving out the information?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was basic common sense that when you are a journalist covering a conflict and you are getting a view of the conflict from one side, that that information has to be treated knowing that it can't be verified and that the persons giving it to you have good reason to possibly manipulate, exaggerate. These are things that we experience all the time. In fact, that was the very early stages of the conflict in the Balkans and it was quite unsophisticated, but it was later to become quite an art form, trying to get a particular view of what was happening portrayed in the international press.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Davies. I'm asking you this because when mentioning the events that took place in November, among other things, you said that the information that was put out by the Croats was sometimes correct and other times not. And you spoke about the occasion when the Old Town was attacked. You heard the explosion of a shell, and they told you that before that three shells had fallen on the town. Do you recall that particular situation?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned the damage done to the monastery in the Old Town on that occasion. Do you happen to remember what extent the damage was in November 1991, what damage was incurred?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw some damage, and it's my non-expert view -- it wasn't so bad that it couldn't be restored. That's not an area that I'm an expert in. It's much easier to say that something has been hit by a shell or a mortar and you have seen this and it's -- it is true. If something's been levelled to the ground, then that's easy to -- or wrecked, then that's easy to describe and verify. But a lot of the damage to monuments in Dubrovnik didn't appear to be of a type that couldn't be repaired. The old walls and some of the buildings appeared to stand up very well to weapons of the 21st century.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Well, can we agree then that in the course of November, that is to say after the fighting that you described in the month of November, that when you toured the Old Town - on the 13th of November, in actual fact, in 1991 - that you were able to see a considerable number of damages, but you say that they weren't serious in the sense of not being able to repair them.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really think that I'm qualified to make that judgement, particularly dealing with buildings as old as that. But I could say, as an observer, that the damage to the buildings and monuments wasn't as bad as I had thought it might be during the assault itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: That means that in November, let's say, in the Old Town, no building had been destroyed or burnt, is that what you mean, completely?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall seeing any building levelled to the ground or destroyed to the point that it couldn't be rebuilt, repaired. But there was considerable damage. And fires had been caused and very old buildings and monuments had been damaged, but again, I don't recall seeing anything that was so badly damaged that it couldn't be restored.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you say that many old buildings and monuments were damaged, does that refer to November 1991 in the Old Town itself?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. I wasn't there in December.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also mentioned having seen Croatian forces on the ground and that on the sea you saw speedboats breaking through the blockade, taking away the wounded, and bringing in ammunition. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: We saw speedboats and we saw them leaving in order to do those things that you've just described. We didn't actually see them doing it, but we did -- we saw them leaving with that intent, and we also used them on occasions to take out pictures, tapes, when the television transmitter in the television station had been destroyed, badly damaged, and we could no longer send out pictures from Dubrovnik itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And tell me, please, the tapes, your report, the footage, who did you hand that over to, or rather, the speedboats taking things outside Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: The speedboats travelled up the coast, landing at pre-arranged places that were still in Croatian hands. And the representative of my company would go to that area and collect the tapes and then would take them back to an office that he had established in Split where he would put together the pictures and the words that we had sent out. It's a crude way of putting together news reports, where you send out the pictures and the words separately with a guide as to what pictures should be placed with what words, but it's a way of getting around problems like the TV transmitter being bombed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davies, I completely understand the problem that you were faced with, and I'm sure that wasn't the first time, in view of the fact that you have reported from many battlefields. But the problem I'm concerned with is Dubrovnik and that whole area, 1991. So my question to you was: Who and where did you hand over this material to? If it was in the Dubrovnik region, who did you hand your tapes over to, your films, for them to be taken out of Dubrovnik in the speedboats?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: My producer, whose name is Sandy McIntyre, took the tapes down to the port and gave them to a Croatian person who was on the speedboat. And when the boat left, we got a message through to our man in Split to go to wherever it was the speedboat was heading for, and it wasn't always the same place, to meet the boat and collect the tape from the person to whom we had given it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, just tell me this: When you say that you handed them over to a Croatian person in the port, in the speedboat, could you tell me which port you mean. The port in the Old Town, the port of Gruz, or some third port perhaps?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think - and it is only think - that it was the port of Gruz. I never did the handing over myself, so I can't be 100 per cent sure. I believe it was Gruz, but that's not to say that it certainly was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Since you're not certain, can you tell me whether those speedboats were to be seen in the port of the Old Town? Did they go there too to perform certain things? Did they operate from the port in the Old Town at all?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, but I do not know for sure. These were very specific, easy-to-recognise boats. They were high-powered speedboats. I don't know, technically they call them "pencil" or something like that, but they have very, very long front ends; they are very, very fast, and the hope was that they could use speed to get through any naval blockade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were they the very fast speedboats of the type - you've just reminded me of this - of the type which were mostly used for trafficking clandestine goods along the seas. The power of the motors and what they looked like, the general speed and power of them, was it the black marketeering type?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite possibly, but I've also seen similar sort of boats used in high-power boat racing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During your stay in Dubrovnik, did you ever happen to hear about a formation, a detachment of armed ships, in fact, to which these speedboats belonged, the ones you've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really. We used to jokingly refer to these speedboats as the Croatian navy. I wasn't aware of ships of any sort with guns on them being used by the Croatians, but that isn't to say it didn't happen. I wasn't aware of that, only these speedboats and the use they were being put to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Have you perhaps heard of the first such speedboat, called Sveti Vlaho, St. Blaise, Ladislav Merkas was commander of that speedboat throughout the war in the Dubrovnik area.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that, either the name of the boat or the name of the commander, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the names of the other speedboats; Jim, Bom, Lude Gude, Dezerter, Formula 4, and so on? Do you know of any of these names?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Those -- this is the first time that I've heard those names.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: During your stay in Dubrovnik, did you hear of the existence of special police units?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really. We heard talk of various units that might have existed on either side, but nothing any more detailed than that. We didn't see any evidence of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: During the last session, I did not quote the exact page of the Milosevic case transcript. I managed to obtain this during the break, though, so I would like to repeat this in connection with my question that had to do with your colleague's stay in hospital. On page 16830 in the Milosevic case, the question was: "Is it correct, Mr. Davies, that in the immediate vicinity of the Dubrovnik hospital there were Croatian forces and that they opened fire at the JNA from those positions?" 16831 is the page of your response. You say: "I don't know about that for sure. I did not see that. Everything I can say is that there was quite a bit of fire from the surrounding area -- from the area around the hospital. I did not see whether this was outgoing fire, but I did hear that there was a mobile mortar positioned there and that it operated very close to that particular place and that it was perhaps involved in this fire. My colleague spent a great deal of time in hospital and he was quite certain that the area around the hospital was under fire for a few days." Does this jog your memory?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does and it also shows me why there was confusion before. The colleague who spent a great deal of time at the hospital was -- wasn't injured or bed-bound or whatever. He used to go to the hospital to check on numbers of casualties and that sort of thing. And he did tell us that he -- there'd been a lot of fire around the hospital. In fact, he was, as I mentioned earlier today, he was injured during one of these exchanges where he was trying to run from the roof of the hospital and damaged his -- damaged his foot. And yes, as I said before, although I didn't witness any of this, my colleague who was there did say that there seemed to be a lot of fire being exchanged around the hospital; not from the hospital but around the hospital. And like some of the other instances we've discussed, that was partly explained by us, though some of it was more conjecture than fact, as being the mobile mortar units and attempts to hit them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me: Since you spent a considerable amount of time in Dubrovnik, did you come across Croatian soldiers in different localities, people who were engaged in war operations in the Dubrovnik area?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: We came across armed Croatians in different areas. I wasn't aware that very many of the people we saw were anything more than militia, if you like, of people who had been armed because of what was happening around Dubrovnik -- as in civilians who had been armed. But yes, I came across them in a number of positions, as I have intimated before; and in particular, the fort on top of Srdj, there were armed Croatians up there; there were armed Croatians just beyond the port of Gruz at the point where the Croats' control ceased; and we saw them, again as we've discussed several times, moving around and being involved in operations to fire their weapons and move again. So yes, we were aware that there were armed Croatians in various different parts of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So we can agree then that you saw people in uniform and also people who were wearing civilian clothing but who nevertheless bore weapons. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Simple answer, yes. Most of the time, though, people with weapons, even the civilians who had been enlisted to this defensive militia, if you like, wore uniforms most of the time. But you did also see people not wearing uniforms who had weapons, small arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Am I right if I say to you in relation to the photograph from Boskovicev Park, the man who is putting a shell into the mortar, who is loading the mortar, so to speak, he is wearing civilian clothes, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to see that again to give you a definite yes or no answer on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D28, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the kind of clothing he's wearing? Can you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking closely at it, it appears to be denim jeans and some sort of a jumper or sweatshirt that is not military camouflage, it appears. It might be clearer on the photograph itself. No, it's actually deceptive. If you look closer at it, I thought that was something like a rugby shirt that he was wearing, but in fact if you look closer, that's probably some sort of body armour protection. It looks rather like a blue flak jacket that he's wearing. I would agree that it is not obvious military uniform, but that does look like some sort of a flak jacket.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: At any rate, you would say that this man was dressed like a civilian. Right? This is civilian clothing, isn't it? You wouldn't say that he was wearing a military uniform or that he had any military insignia.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. It's civilian clothing, not military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Last time -- excuse me. Last time you mentioned to us a man by the name of Mario Peci who got killed in November, if I'm not mistaken, in the area of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that you knew him personally and that he was a member of the Croatian army. Right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I knew him because I met him and I talked to him for quite some time. And I met him on Srdj, in the fort, but I didn't know him beyond having met him on that particular day. As for whether he was a member of the Croatian army, he was a member of the Croatian defence, but he wasn't any form of regular army. The reason I remember him so well is that he owned a restaurant and a discotheque in Dubrovnik and spoke excellent English because of his work with tourists and was quite a -- he was different. He was quite a jovial character and we talked to him quite a lot. We interviewed him as part of one of the films that we were making. But he wasn't a -- he wasn't regular army. He, like most of the other people we met, were -- was a civilian involved in the tourist trade, really, who had been enlisted in a defence force, had been given weapons, and the last time we saw him alive he had a mortar, a single mortar, and was moving it from the side of Mount Srdj to somewhere where it was going to be used. And he was killed that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, while watching the film that was shown during the first day of your testimony in this courtroom, the narrator, the reporter who was actually following the images and explaining what was happening, was that you in that specific situation, in that particular footage?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I am going to refer to the transcript of your report, that is to say what you were actually saying in the report. You say, when talking about the bombing of the Napoleonic fort: "The exchange of gunfire was not completely one way because mortar shells were fired from town, those that could not reach the federal artillery batteries hidden amongst the trees on the top of Mount Zarkovica." On the basis of what do you infer that, that these shells could not reach the positions of the federal army?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply that they were falling short of that position and I didn't believe, and it was only my presumption, but I didn't believe that they could have been deliberately targeted at the mountainside just below, gun positions that I could quite clearly see were firing into Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Where were they firing from, from Dubrovnik itself?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that occasion, I didn't know. From subsequent experience, it would make sense that they were being fired from somewhere near the Belvedere Hotel, because that is the closest that you can get to those positions. And it did seem that the only chance of hitting those positions was to get about as close as it was possible for the Croatians to get, which was near the coast alongside the Belvedere Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davies, I'm going to phrase my question this way: Do you agree with me that at the moment when you were giving this description that actually followed the images on the film, you did not know the exact positions that the Croatian artillery was shooting from. You don't know whether it's a mortar or a gun. You don't know the calibre of the weapon involved. You don't know the parameters of that artillery piece. You don't know what the charges were, what kind of ordnance was used. You don't know the exact range of the artillery pieces involved. You don't know whether the sights are in proper order on these weapons that were used to fire at the JNA. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree that that was the situation a lot of the time. It would be impossible to know that long list of things that you have just set out there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me then that your statement they could not reach the positions of the other side, are simply -- is simply an assumption, since you do not have all the knowledge required for a qualified statement, all the things I referred to in my previous question?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with you that it is an assumption, but I think it's a pretty fair assumption to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In your view, then, would it also be reasonable to presume that those who were actually doing the firing, that is to say the Croatian artillery, could make a mistake, like anybody can make a mistake? Also, as you put it yourself, when they often change positions while firing - that is to say once they fire they immediately move the mortar away, take it to another position - perhaps there is not enough time for the sights to be put in order. Perhaps that could be reason to assume that, just like you assumed that they did not have the proper range to reach the positions on top. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you pause. Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I would object. The question doesn't seem to make any sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think what is apparent from the question is the proposition is being posed for your comment, Mr. Davies: Could the mortars have been not properly sighted because they had just been recently moved, or could those sighting them have made a mistake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the answer to that would be that, yes, it is possible that the sights could not have been properly set because of what was happening; yes, it is possible that they made a mistake; and yes, if we're going down that road, it is possible that they could have been deliberately targeting a bit of barren hillside below where gun positions were firing at them. It is possible but it seemed unlikely. If I'm being asked to put an opinion, as I appear to be, then if I, day after day, watch exchanges - because there were exchanges, one-sided though they were - where one side seems not able, for various reasons, to hit the other side's positions, then I -- with what I do see with my own eyes that these weapons they have are not particularly high calibre, I think it's a fair conclusion to reach that they are not able to reach those positions. But all of those possibilities that have been raised could be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davies, in relation to this, I did not ask you about the most important thing, perhaps. Do you know about how well trained the mortar operators were on the Croatian side, those who were firing the mortar shells from the Croatian side?
