You will agree with me that this is a very important thing.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the answer to your question is no, I don't know how well trained the mortar operators were.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And do you agree that along with the other elements that you did not know about and that we referred to just now, this was yet another very relevant element, the degree of training, that is, when we are talking about precision of targeting?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is relevant, but it won't change my opinion and the opinion that I voiced in the report that I made, that they simply weren't able to reach the targets they were firing at.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me, Mr. Davies, in terms of this last matter, the degree of training that the mortar operators had, and all the other elements we referred to earlier on that you did not know about, that if we look at all of this together, these are very important matters in order to make a realistic assessment as to why shells in a particular case did not reach their target? They fell before the actual target that was being engaged.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, they may be relevant factors. Of course training to use a weapon is extremely important, but when you've witnessed something happening over a period of days again and again and you've had an opportunity to at least gauge the sort of fire power that exists on both sides, I think it's still fair to come to the conclusion that these things were not hitting their targets because most of the time they weren't able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I'm going to give you yet another element in terms of food for thought. Do you believe that there is a distinction between the two following things: A protected dug-in artillery piece of the JNA, which is dug-in according to all military rules; and on the other hand the Croatian artillery pieces that you described, that is to say firing fast, moving away fast, shooting yet again from this other locality? Are these important elements when we talk about the exchange of fire, when we talk about precision and so on and so forth? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they ought to be factors. If you're asking if a professional military properly dug-in, properly trained, with powerful weapons ought to perform better than a militia with less powerful weapons, not properly dug-in, then yes, the JNA ought to outperform the Croatian defenders of Dubrovnik every time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You've gone a little further in your answer from my actual question. But don't you think that I gave you a lot of elements which were unknown categories? But you draw the conclusion in your report that can be called a simple one, and that is that the Croatian artillery at a given point in time was not able to reach the position, the JNA positions because they had -- didn't have the kind of weapons the JNA had. They had weaker weapons. That is your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was my conclusion, but you can add to it the list of things that you were putting forward, the being properly trained and dug-in and professional, that would all add to the same conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, don't you think you've rather dealt with this point more than adequately?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just one more question, with the Court's indulgence, on this matter, and then I'll move on to another topic and I think I'll be able to complete the cross-examination quickly after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davies, I've been asking you all this for us to be able to compare a situation in which you have a very effective image of the Croatian artillery hitting the munitions warehouse at Zarkovica and that this led to a great explosion, a big explosion. Do you agree that that was very effective, an effective image from the journalistic point of view, from the aspect of your profession, in fact?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was very effective. And -- because it was so unusual, that made it even more an effective tool to, if you like, show that, although one-sided, this wasn't just one side bombarding another with the other not defending at all; there were occasional successes on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, I respect that explanation of yours, because it stands. However, what I'm interested in with respect to the previous questions and the topic we were discussing, it is this: If they managed to hit the warehouse at Zarkovica, do you know exactly from what position the hits were made in order to hit the warehouse at Zarkovica? Where were they shooting from? Or let me be more specific: What were the positions from which, the exact positions, from which the Croatian artillery was able to have a range reaching that target, the JNA targets? So what positions did they have giving them a range in which they were able to hit their target? Do you have any information or facts and figures about that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Not at all. I didn't know the position that those -- that that particular shot, the one that hit the JNA position, I couldn't tell where it was fired from. And I wouldn't know what the range of the weapon that fired that shell, what its range was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When in your report you filmed the Belvedere Hotel, you as the reporter say that the -- it seems that the guns were targeting the gun nest, Croatian gun nest, at the Belvedere Hotel along the coast. You said that refugees had been put up at the Belvedere Hotel. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So in the Belvedere Hotel, were there soldiers of the Croatian army, apart from this gun nest that you mention? So were there any soldiers there accommodated in and around the Belvedere Hotel?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether there were -- the Belvedere Hotel was, because of its position, was very difficult to get to. I think we visited it once or twice. We didn't see Croatian military there on the occasions that we visited it. But because we heard either mortars or artillery being used from there on at least one occasion, we know that they were operating from there. I don't know -- I mean, when you say "gun nest," that's your phrase. I don't know that it wasn't necessarily one or two mortars that had been moved into that position, fired, and moved again. I don't know if it was a permanent military presence there. We didn't see Croatian soldiers when we visited the Belvedere Hotel. It could be we only visited it once during the entire period we were there, possibly twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: During your stay in Dubrovnik, did you happen to see any other places, any other positions, where the civilian and the army mixed, civilian positions, military positions, and operations from those positions or near the positions where there were any civilians in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it -- Dubrovnik's a relatively small place. The use of weapons almost anywhere in the region would mean that civilians would be not very far away. The simple answer to your question is: We were aware of guns being fired or mortars being fired from alongside our hotel, which had civilians in it, alongside the Belvedere Hotel on occasion, and there were refugees in there. I didn't see anything cruder than that. I didn't see any what we now describe as human shield type operations, where you deliberately put weapons in the middle of a civilian target so that nobody will fire at it. But the instances that I've told you about certainly happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I do believe you. But I didn't mention any human shield either, and if we're talking about a human shield then that implies the direct positioning of humans in front of artillery pieces. But I don't think either of us mentioned human shields in actual fact. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: However, what you just talked about and something that was brought up on several occasions, that in the hotel that you were accommodated in, there were civilians put up, too, and the observer European mission as well, and that the Croats were quite nearby the hotel and firing from there, does that mean that they would be attracting fire from the opposite side as well? And for that reason, because the opposite side was firing at the fire power positions of the Croatian side, that there could have been mistakes or movement in the shots where innocent people would have been casualties? Is that a realistic situation, too?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's always a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: When you described the 6th of November and say that the main target of attack was Srdj, you also said that the town was patrolled by, or rather, that cannons, gunboats around Dubrovnik also opened fire, the ones that were patrolling the area around Dubrovnik, that there was gunfire coming from gunboats. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- without looking at notes, I'd find that difficult to give you a straight yes or no answer to that on November the 6th. I do remember days when gunboats and other boats fired, but I couldn't definitively say that November the 6th was one of those days. I do remember that November the 11th was a day when the gunboats and other boats were particularly active in firing at Dubrovnik. I would have to look back at some of my work to see what happened on the 6th.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you. The last sentence of your statement given to the investigators, speaking about the 6th of November reads as follows: "The town was shelled by gunboats, which were patrolling around town, and there were many shells that fell close to the Dubrovnik hospital." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: That sounds -- that sounds true, and at the time I made that statement I would have been able to -- just before then, to look at the relevant notes made at the time. But I can now start to envisage the report that we sent out at that time which did show shells dropping relatively close to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what I wanted to hear from you, and let me continue from my previous question with respect to the abuse of locations populated by civilians, and the hospital is precisely one such facility and location. So would it be true to say, then, that the firing of Croatian artillery from positions in the immediate vicinity of a hospital or the Argentina Hotel, for example, would be along those lines, that this kind of operation represents a real danger and jeopardises those facilities and the people in them? Would you agree with me there?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with you inasmuch as if you're saying that firing weapons from relatively close to civilian populations and a building like a hospital raises the possibility of those being hit, then yes, that is an obvious danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what I was asking you about. Thank you. Is it true and correct that, according to your report, the first shell during November, as you said, fell on the Old Town on the 10th of November, in fact?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: According to you - and you say you remember that because of your own birthday - that the strongest shelling during November was on the 11th. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And on that particular day you yourself -- on the day of the shelling, and operations from both sides you followed from the walls of the Old Town. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a good part of that day, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, please -- tell me, when moving around the Old Town during those days, that is to say the days there was no shelling, did you happen to come across any armed persons?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that there were people with small arms around the Old Town. I didn't see anything larger than small arms, and I don't recall seeing anything that you would associate with some sort of military activity inasmuch as you might see one or two people wandering and they had small arms. But I didn't see gun positions or any preparations being made or anything involving firearms. But on occasions, I did see people in uniform, and some of those people would be carrying small arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you say that some of those people carried small arms or personal weapons, would an automatic rifle rank among those, a pistol; is that the kind of weaponry you saw them with?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: A pistol would be what I'm referring to. It's possible that somebody might have a rifle, but that's not the image that comes to my mind. That would have been a rare site. I'm really referring to, as you say, personal weapons, a pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: However, at the beginning today I asked you, based on your film and the situation when you filmed the hit at Zarkovica and you were in the Old Town yourself, I asked you about the five men who were to be seen behind a wall in the Old Town, and I said that two of them were wearing uniforms and that you could see an automatic rifle that one of them had. And this is on your own footage. Now, do you allow for the fact that there might have been people with other kinds of weapons, or rather, rifles and not just pistols moving around the Old Town? Would that jog your memory?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's -- of course it's possible, but again I would have to say we spent a lot of time in and around the Old Town. And we would have -- if there had been any significant weaponry on the walls and certainly anybody using them, whether it was small arms or anything larger, I believe we would have been aware of it, we would have seen it, and we would have filmed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you this because on page 9, paragraph 1, of your statement you say that: "I would see every day a Croatian defender because they worked in the Argentina Hotel," or words to that effect, and they didn't have any special clothing because they weren't regular soldiers. They were ordinary people who dealt in tourism. They would be given weapons from the police station and they were small, old rifles and pistols. I think that paragraph contains quite a bit of what I asked you previously. You say they were ordinary people, very ordinary people, with tourism background, and they came to the hotel as Croatian defenders. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not really. What I meant was that we would see people working at the hotel, and later in the day they would leave to go and do whatever military role they had been given. I can remember instances of seeing the man who served coffee at breakfast wearing a dark jacket and a dickey bow tie, later in the day with a camouflage jacket - no other uniform I don't think than a camouflage jacket - and a not very impressive rifle up on Srdj. And he would live his life with doing his shift at work and then going to do his shift with the militia or defence or whatever we call it. I wouldn't want to give the impression that what I saw at the hotel was people with military roles doing military jobs at the hotel. These were just people who worked at the hotel that also had a military life.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, would this be a good moment to break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I thought that you were at the end of your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I forgot to say previously that I promise to finish very soon after the break, after we resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's what you said at about five to midday. We will adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davies, I assume that this film that you brought along to The Hague this time is the original, the original that you took then in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, it's the original that was recorded in London as it was fed in to my company's headquarters on the 14th of November. It's the version that they recorded and then later broadcast on that same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, this is a recording that your company made on the basis of the material that you sent from Dubrovnik. Your company made this film, they edited it, played it as such, and the material of your company that was telecast in this form was then handed over to the OTP. Right? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's partly correct. This is the recording that was made in London of material that was fed in from somewhere in Serbia where it was being sent via satellite. It wasn't edited in London. They simply recorded the broadcast intact and then later broadcast it on television. So it hasn't been edited or interfered with, it has simply been recorded in from the satellite and then broadcast on television, and it still has the original clock on it, which is the way that we would have started the material as we put it together in Dubrovnik. That is something that was missing from the copy that we saw last time, which I still don't know how it was acquired. I think you would have to ask the Prosecution that. But that didn't have the first few seconds, the clock that comes first, and then the first few seconds of the first shot, and it was also curtailed rather abruptly a few seconds before the actual report had finished. But in every other aspect other quality, they are the same. The version I brought to the Court is simply the perfect one with the extra few seconds at either end.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, this film that you brought in, is that film from the boxes with the notes that you referred to last time?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is film from the archives of my company, which keeps a recording of every report that it takes in from the satellite and later broadcasts. The relevance of the boxes and the notes, these are the details that would have helped me put together the script for the film that I have here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me something else in relation to this film: If we look at this version that you brought in now where this clock can be seen at the outset and the material that you sent from Dubrovnik, is this identical or is there something missing?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I asked you last time, if you remember, apart from this film do you have any other recordings or films from the time you reported from the Dubrovnik area? If I'm not mistaken, you said that you had four or five such films, and you said that you kept them in the boxes with the notes. That is to say the boxes that are marked and it probably says which are the films involved.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. That's a little bit complicated. Yes, I told you that this long report wasn't the only report that we sent out of Dubrovnik; there were several others. And I also told you that in putting together the words, the script that you hear, the narration is probably the better word, on these reports, that I would have used my memory, notes that I made on the day, and also notes that appeared on the boxes of the tapes. And again, to try and make that more easy to understand, each tape like this one which is the 11-, 12-minute report that we saw, or very similar to the one we saw when I was here last, this is put together from, it could be 10, 12 other tapes that are filmed over a period of days. You take out the -- use the pictures you want to use and put together a report that all comes together on tape. On many of the boxes there would have been a sheet of white paper here with lines and room for you to write down notes of what's on it, the people you talked to, perhaps a rough summary of what happened on it. And it's just another form of notebook. You use it along with your notes in putting together the narration. I hope that's helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me just one more thing in relation to the actual film you brought in today. Is that the way it was made, as you mentioned, from these 10 or 12 cassettes: Material was chosen, selected, edited, and then sent as a comprehensive report from Dubrovnik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's exactly right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps bring in any of those cassettes today out of which you extracted this footage that is contained in this report, this original cassette that you brought in today? Did you bring any of those 10 or 12 cassettes with that material? Did you bring any of that with you today?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. It's not normal practice to keep -- the technical phrase for those tapes is "rushes." And it's not normal practice to keep rushes for a long time after an event. As you can imagine, we're talking about 12 boxes like this, maybe, to make one piece. And during the course of an assignment you might make -- send back 10 or 12, broadcast each one, taking as many tapes, 10 or 12 tapes, to make each individual report. If you start to do the sums, you end up with hundreds and hundreds of tapes. And that's just one assignment of one reporter. So our archives, after a period of time, only keep the reports that are broadcast as a record. And there's a legal obligation that they should do so as well. It's quite rare for them to keep the original rushes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes. Very well, Mr. Davies. I understand that. If this report that you brought in here today, if it contains 11 minutes of material, tell me, approximately how much material do these 10 or 12 cassettes contain, the rushes as you call them? How much material do they contain, approximately?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: 150 minutes, 200 minutes. You must understand that something like filming artillery firing and the few seconds that you see on the news where there's an explosion and the damage that's caused, quite often the camera will have been trained on that spot for 10, 15 minutes just to get that one image. And if you multiply that over and over again for every single thing you see in the report, it's a lot of material. It's one of the most time-consuming parts of our job is condensing it into a fair reflection of what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I agree that the viewers of your television certainly would not find it interesting to watch that abundance of material, as you described it. But am I right if I say that if a report of about 11 minutes was taken out of 150 or 200 minutes in total and if that is what we saw here, would I be correct if I put it that way?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It would be something around that. Each of these tapes, if they're full, can hold 20 to 30 minutes of material. And sometimes you put a report together from as many as 10 tapes. So you can do the sums. Some will only have a limited amount of material; some will be almost full. So it's a lot of material.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Davies.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have completed the cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rodic. Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Davies.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We'll be brief. Have you reviewed that tape you brought with you today?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And is that the complete tape you sent?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is, even including the clock, which is the start of the piece that we put together, but something that isn't broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And is that a fair and accurate depiction of what you saw on those days?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is. Yes, I am very proud of being able to say that that's what we saw. That was our interpretation of what was happening there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the tape that you had previously seen when you were here to testify approximately a month and a half ago, was all of the information on that tape included on this tape which you brought today?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is. There's -- the only difference is an extra few seconds at the start and an extra few seconds at the end. It doesn't look truncated or abruptly finished, and it is the way that it will have been both put together and broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: With the assistance of the audio/visual room, could we run the first 30 seconds and the last 30 seconds of that tape, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Mr. Davies, having just reviewed that, that is the complete tape?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the complete tape, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We would like to offer that at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that will be Prosecution Exhibit P92, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In addition, as a matter of housekeeping, for the record could we officially offer the statement of Ellen Gardner in relation to the other tape which was tendered this morning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be -- yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence has an objection in relation to this statement. If the written statement is being admitted into evidence, regardless of what it has to do with, if there is no live testimony to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. The Defence was the ones who, on page 638 and 655, made two requests for the provenance of the tape. They did it at that portion in the cross-examination and then before we closed for the day, they again requested the provenance of that tape. It's a -- we have responded; we have filed a document. It does relate to their request, it does relate to the tape. It's not a significant document, and we would like to enter it at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you maintain your objection, Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. One question had to do with the other question, which is only natural in this case. Mr. Davies during the examination-in-chief and during the cross-examination explained to us, and now he brought us yet another tape, that there is a lack of material that he called -- that he referred to as a few seconds at the beginning and a few seconds at the end. Mr. Davies gave an explanation and he brought the original tape, which was played here now, and it explains the lack of this material in the recording. The Defence certainly did receive from Mr. Davies what it wanted to. This film, which was introduced as P19, and this new film that was introduced now includes the seconds that were missing. And all of this was taken out of the 150 or 200 minutes that Mr. Davies recorded in Dubrovnik. Therefore, we maintain our objection, that is that this kind of statement should not be admitted into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rodic. I would normally see some significance in what you are submitting, but on this occasion, as it has been produced in response to your request and as it really does not introduce anything of any significant difference from what we have heard from Mr. Davies except to provide some of the background to his evidence, I think it would be appropriate for it to be received. So we will admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That statement will be Exhibit P91, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Just a few questions, Mr. Davies. You were questioned about the explosion on Zarkovica, allegedly by Croatian fire. Are there any other possibilities which could have caused that explosion? For example, can you rule out sabotage? Can you rule out accident or some sort of mishap with --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What my colleague Mr. Weiner is asking about now goes beyond speculation, because the film footage and also the narration that explains the images, and also during the examination-in-chief and several times during the cross-examination the witness confirmed that he personally followed this and that the explosion at Zarkovica was caused by Croatian artillery fire. Therefore, it is inappropriate to deal with it in re-direct, especially to speculate in this way with inaccurate information, because the witness unequivocally said several times what caused the explosion at Zarkovica. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, I had occasion to suggest to Mr. Rodic that this issue had been more than adequately covered in the course of his cross-examination, and really I don't know that we would be helped by you adding even more conjecture on to that which was put before us. So perhaps you will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you were questioned about flags -- and you were questioned about your statement and you were questioned about flags. In your statement on page 7, the second full paragraph, the first sentence it says: "The Croatians never thought that the Old Town would ever become a target of attack, as it was an UNESCO protected site in its entirety and The Hague Convention flags were flying over most of the buildings." Do you recall Hague Convention flags?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall flags, blue and white flags, and that they depicted the fact that it was a protected site. I probably would not have thought or known that that was The Hague Convention flag at the time I saw it. The first time that I saw it it was just a flag that indicated that it was a protected site and it was hugely visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And one more topic. You said that you could not recall any provocative action coming from the town. That was part of an answer during cross-examination. Were you referring to the Old Town in that answer?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly I was referring to the Old Town. I wasn't aware of provocative action, and I believe that I would probably have been aware had it happened, though I couldn't say that I would certainly have known. But I was also talking in general terms. I wasn't aware of provocative action that started the conflict of any individual day. To be fair, I'm not sure that I would have been in a position to have known who started what most of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But, sir, would you agree that you never observed any outgoing fire from the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never observed any outgoing fire from the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Davies, the time has come when you are at the end of your evidence. We must thank you very much for your two attendances here and the assistance you've given and wish you well on your journey. And you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is it for the day, is it, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I apologise that it seems that's it than more than the day; today and tomorrow. We have a bit of a logistics problem with the next witness, and due to that we don't feel it necessary -- we don't feel we should be placing him on the witness stand tomorrow because of some certain problems. If the Court would like, I can go into private session on the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What you're proposing then is that we adjourn until Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. We're all set for next week. We have witnesses Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday, as required, but we have a bit of a problem for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that is clearly understood by everybody. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if that is what the situation is, then the Defence would ask for the following: Could we know already at this stage who will be called on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday so that we could see how much time we need for examining these witnesses. Because if it's Mr. Janicot on Tuesday, his evidence will probably be lengthy and he has to testify only at a certain point in time because his schedule is pretty tight. So we really don't want witnesses to be coming in and not be heard over these three days that we have left for our work. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, can you assist us with the witnesses?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Witness A. And on Tuesday and Wednesday, Mr. Janicot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have to be very economical in time with Mr. Janicot if Mr. Petrovic's concern is well based.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We accept his concerns and we'll do the best we can to move him as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to subscribe what has been -- to what has been said so far, see we have a problem with tomorrow, and the Defence would kindly ask our colleagues from the Prosecution, in terms of next Wednesday, the 10th, because we will be adjourned on the 11th onwards, could they please tell us who will be testifying on the 18th and 19th of March? I mean the day when we finish, could we please receive information on who the witnesses for the 18th and 19th will be. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, I'd ask that attention be given to that so that we might know before we adjourn for the week next Wednesday afternoon who it is that will be before us the following week when we resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That shouldn't be any problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just eliminating you from the record, Mr. Weiner. We will adjourn now until Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: at 1.35 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 8th day of March, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.
